In Finland, employers must insure their employees against accidents at work, and the insurers'
records of every compensated accident are compiled into national statistics by Statistics Finland
and the Finnish Workers' Compensation Center. This notebook uses accidents from 2008 to 2024 by
industry, age, sex, place and outcome, the European (ESAW) classification of how accidents happen,
and rates per worker and per hour worked. Read the module [README](../README.md) and
[data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/fi-statfin-work-accidents/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name, ...) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           ...)
}

# Accidents by year, employment status, place, outcome, sex, age group and industry
accidents <- read_module("tidy", "accidents.csv.gz")
# Wage and salary earners' accidents per 100,000 workers and per million hours, 2018 onward
rates <- read_module("tidy", "rates.csv")
# Workplace accidents by the European classification of how they happened
esaw <- read_module("tidy", "esaw_causes.csv")
# Farmers' accidents (at least 4 days off work) per 100,000 insured farmers
farmers <- read_module("tidy", "farmers.csv")

# Order the outcome categories from least to most serious
outcome_levels <- c("0-3 days", "4-6 days", "7-14 days", "15-30 days", "31-90 days",
                    "91-180 days", "181 days or more", "Disability pension", "Fatal")
accidents <- accidents |>
  mutate(outcome = factor(outcome, outcome_levels),
         four_plus_days = outcome != "0-3 days")
```

Each row of `accidents` is a **number of accidents** for one combination of the variables. Add
rows up with `sum(accidents)`, not `n()`.

# Part 1. Trends

```{r trend}
by_year <- accidents |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(all_accidents = sum(accidents),
            four_plus_days = sum(accidents[four_plus_days]),
            fatal_at_work = sum(accidents[outcome == "Fatal" & place != "Commuting"]),
            fatal_commuting = sum(accidents[outcome == "Fatal" & place == "Commuting"]))
by_year

by_year |>
  select(year, `All accidents` = all_accidents, `At least 4 days off work` = four_plus_days) |>
  pivot_longer(-year) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Accidents at work and while commuting, Finland", x = NULL, y = "Accidents",
       colour = NULL)

rates |>
  filter(section == "Total", sex == "Total", place == "All") |>
  select(year, workers, accidents_4plus_days, per_100000_workers)
```

**Questions**

1. How did the number of accidents change from 2008 to 2024? What happened in 2020, and why?
2. About two thirds of accidents cause three days off work or less. Many countries count only
   accidents with more than three days off. Why do you think that threshold is common, and what do
   you lose by using it?
3. Finland has between 20 and 55 fatal accidents a year (counting commuting). Why is it hard to
   study trends in such small numbers, and how could you make the comparison more stable?

# Part 2. Who is injured?

```{r who}
accidents |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  group_by(sex, place) |>
  summarise(accidents = sum(accidents), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = place, values_from = accidents)

accidents |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(share_women = sum(accidents[sex == "Female"]) / sum(accidents),
            share_commuting = sum(accidents[place == "Commuting"]) / sum(accidents)) |>
  pivot_longer(-year) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Share of accidents among women and while commuting", x = NULL, y = NULL,
       colour = NULL)

accidents |>
  filter(year == 2024, four_plus_days) |>
  count(age_group, wt = accidents, name = "accidents") |>
  mutate(share = round(accidents / sum(accidents), 3))
```

**Questions**

1. In 2024, did more women or men have commuting accidents, and accidents at the workplace? Why
   might the pattern differ between the two?
2. Women's share of accidents has grown. Give one explanation about changes in jobs and one about
   reporting.
3. Without the number of workers in each age group, can you say which age group has the highest
   risk? What would you need?

# Part 3. Industries and rates

```{r industries}
rates |>
  filter(year == 2024, sex == "Total", place == "All", !section %in% c("Total", "X", "U")) |>
  select(section, section_name, workers, accidents_4plus_days, per_100000_workers) |>
  arrange(desc(per_100000_workers))

rates |>
  filter(year == 2024, sex == "Total", place == "At work (including traffic while working)",
         !is.na(per_million_hours), section != "X") |>
  ggplot(aes(per_million_hours, fct_reorder(section_name, per_million_hours))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Accidents at work (4+ days off) per million hours worked, 2024",
       x = "Per million hours", y = NULL)

accidents |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  count(industry, wt = accidents, name = "accidents", sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)
```

**Questions**

1. Which industries have the highest and lowest accident rates per 100,000 workers? Which have the
   most accidents? Why are the two lists different?
2. Rates per worker and per million hours rank industries in a similar order but not the same.
   When would the rate per hour be the better measure? (Think about part-time work.)
3. The "Local government sector" (municipal employees, such as care workers, teachers and
   maintenance staff) has more accidents than any industry. Why do the statistics show it as a
   sector rather than by industry, and what problem does that create for comparing industries?

# Part 4. How do accidents happen?

The European Statistics on Accidents at Work (ESAW) describe each accident by what the worker was
doing (activity), what went wrong (deviation), how the worker was hurt (contact), the injury and
the part of the body. These tables cover workplace accidents of wage and salary earners with at
least four days off work.

```{r esaw}
esaw |>
  filter(year == 2024, sex == "Total") |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  mutate(share = round(accidents / sum(accidents, na.rm = TRUE), 3)) |>
  slice_max(accidents, n = 3) |>
  select(variable, category, accidents, share)

esaw |>
  filter(variable == "Deviation", sex != "Total", year >= 2022) |>
  group_by(sex, category) |>
  summarise(accidents = sum(accidents), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = accidents / sum(accidents)) |>
  ggplot(aes(share, fct_reorder(category, share), fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "What went wrong: deviation, 2022 to 2024", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. What is the most common deviation, contact and type of injury? Describe a typical accident in
   one sentence.
2. Which deviations are more common among women and which among men? Relate this to their jobs.
3. Choose the most common deviation and propose two prevention measures, at different levels of the

# Part 5. How serious are accidents?

```{r severity}
accidents |>
  filter(year >= 2022) |>
  count(outcome, wt = accidents, name = "accidents") |>
  mutate(share = round(accidents / sum(accidents), 4))

accidents |>
  filter(year >= 2015, outcome == "Fatal") |>
  count(place, wt = accidents, name = "fatal")

accidents |>
  filter(year >= 2015, outcome == "Fatal", place != "Commuting") |>
  count(section_name, wt = accidents, name = "fatal", sort = TRUE) |>
  head(6)
```
